MOTOROLA XOOM Android Tablet (10.1-Inch, 32GB, Wi-Fi) I used to think tablet computers were just for dorks like that guy on Modern Family and for people that want everyone to see how hip and up-to-date they are. But after nabbing a pile of these for the one team of surveyors at work, I'm pleasantly surprised to see how many real business applications these can tackle.

I won't go into too much detail - there are legions of people contributing to forums and reviews on such matters. What I do hate, however - and this is why it gets only four stars - is that the SD card is still not write-enabled. My buddy working for Google swears he has a software-enabled version that does, but the public does not. Yet, at least. So what's the hold up?, 'cause that is a serious deal-breaker.

On the other hand, Apple's version doesn't even have an SD card slot. Heck, it has nothing that isn't proprietary. iPad was never on the table for me, and probably never will be. Why anyone would go that direction when open source is available cheaper is beyond me. Anyway, to each his own.

My only other issue is that it kept resetting itself on me during casual browsing, driving me nuts, even after a factory reset with no futher modifications. After installing a new browser, I no longer have that problem, thank God.

text_fidelity_a:
GRADO SR80e Prestige Series Headphones The first thing I noted when I listened to these much-celebrated headphones (at least the Prestige line at any rate) is how incredibly exaggerated the low-end is. While getting that kind of bass response from a headphone driver is impressive, showing it off at the expense of fidelity is not something I particularly care for. When using these on a device where a DAC is involved, such as an iPad, I have to use the 'bass reducer' EQ profile on the device or the sound will otherwise will be muddy with distortion. I am sure this has a lot to do with the dinky amplifier inside the iPad being unable to fully drive the the whopping 32 ohms of resistance the SR80e pushes back with. As a rule, underpowered amplifiers are what ruin the drivers inside speakers or headphones so when you hear distortion it means your amplifier is underpowered when matched with the driver and you need to change one of those two things. When you hear distortion from a crappy amplifier that's the sound of your speakers being slowly ruined so you really want to avoid this. (I always have a sad chuckle when some punk is walking the streets with ghetto blaster at maximum volume and the sound is atrocious- little does he know that what people are annoyed by is not the volume, but the distortion! Plus he's ruining his equipment.)

Using the SR80e with a mobile device is a case where an external headphone amplifier would be highly desirable, if not required, so this is a bit of an ask. I have not had a lot of success with the in-line amplifiers designed to run off of the device's power (specifically the Lightning-DAC-and-amplifier combos that you can buy to replace the dongle that Apple ships with their new iPhones) where I played recordings which have very high amplitude levels. For these recordings, the distortion is intolerable even though records at a nominal recording level sound great. The lack of gain control is a real problem with these gadgets- something that is de-facto on any headphone amp that you don't put in your pocket. Therefore, you'll be reduced to using headphones like these at home or work, which is where I use mine.

The fact that you have to significantly alter the EQ profile of your audio player to even have these cans reproduce a sound that is remotely like the original recording violates "high fidelity" by definition. Compare this to a sound engineer style headphone set like Sony MDR Pros which are designed to reproduce the source signal as accurately as possible. This is what "high fidelity" actually means. Some people may not like this and will end up using some artificial bass boost on their device to compensate, which the MDRs will gladly deliver. Most people who listen to popular music are generally accustomed to excessive bass. If that is the sort of listener that you are, then these headphones are for you because once you get the SR80s tuned properly, the sound these cans deliver is very impressive. Very. Impressive.

Unfortunately, when using an IOS device, playing this profile with even high end earbuds like the UE Triple Fis, the sound will be tinny, so toggling between the two modes by way of a shortcut would be a nice bonus, but as it stands I have to go deep into the preferences to change this setting. Therefore, I would only recommend these headphones if you intend to use them in a stationary location. Since these are very high resistance earphones (even higher than most loudspeakers for that matter) you really ought to get an headphone amplifier if you want these to shine.

One other issue is with the minimalist foam cup pads. While they are comfy, they do not block sound in or out whatsoever, so if you use them in a noisy office you will be annoyed at how loud you have to play these to drown out ambient noise. Also, your workmates will probably be annoyed by the bleed through. I ended up getting a different cup pad kit which is marginally better, but it changes the fit somewhat so it takes a little fiddling to get them to sit on your skull around your ears evenly. Otherwise, the headphones are incredibly comfortable as they are very lightweight, which is surprising considering the size of the driver. Grado has found the sweet spot between having a massive (and heavy) drive coil magnet and being featherweight, even if I might take issue with their choices about fidelity reproduction.

Tl;DR: If you really like your sound overcharged with bass, these are the headphones for you. Otherwise, if you are looking for a quality but moderately priced pair of headphones, you might be better off with a more reference-style set like the Sony MDRs.
text_fidelity_b: GRADO SR80e Prestige Series Headphones

text_fidelity_a:
KINESIS Freestyle2 USB Keyboard for Mac (9" Standard Separation), Black Overall this keyboard is great. The keys feel nice and they're quiet but not too quiet or soft or squishy. Enjoy typing on this keyboard, pushing the keys seems to take minimal effort and overall it's great.

The best part about the keyboard is that it separates and having the ability to give it a little separation is great. I miss it when I don't have it and it helps avoid torquing the wrists when you are typing. I also love the feel of the keys.

Now before my minor complaints understand two things: (1) I really like this keyboard and despite what I would consider minor defects, I would definitely buy another one. (2) please excuse the fact that I like my keyboards to be consistent and while Apple may not make the *best* keyboards I do use a laptop and I am used to their keyboard layout and feel.

The biggest thing that annoyed me when I purchased this keyboard was the positioning of the ⌘ (command) key. It seems to be shifted over a bit from what I'm used to. Normally I would hit ⌘ with my thumb but it's a little touch to do that on this one given the position of it. It's just something I'm having to get used to.

One minor downside to the keyboard is that the function key doesn't work the same way as the default apple keyboard, rather, the `fn` key is a toggle. I prefer for fn to work as a modifier because that is what I am used to on my laptop keyboard.

Another minor problem is the styling on the caps lock key. Like many people, I remap my caps lock to ctrl and and thus want caps lock to be a normal button. However, on this keyboard the caps lock key is missing the right part of the key so that you don't accidentally hit it when typing the `a` key.

Finally, the escape key and '`' (back tick) keys are in weird positions. The escape key is not as bad as the backtick. There is just something about the distance that I must go that is different from what I'm used to and I have been consistently hitting the `1` key instead. Life goes on.
text_fidelity_b: KINESIS Freestyle2 USB Keyboard for Mac (9" Standard Separation), Black

text_fidelity_a:
KZ ZS10 Pro, Linsoul 4BA+1DD 5 Driver in Ear Monitor, HiFi Metal Earphones, with Stainless Steel Faceplate, 2 Pin Detachable Cable (Without Mic, Black) Best sounding in-ear headphones I've ever heard, by a mile. I've owned the Bang and Olufsen H3, Sony XBA H1, Klipsch S4, X7, X6i, 1More Dual Drivers, Beats by Dr Dre Tour (wired), and Monster Cable's Jamz and Turbines.

The bass has lots of range and goes DEEP, in some tracks it even reminds me of my Kicker CVR 12' car subwoofer I used to blast about 15 years ago. It is not quite that overpowering, of course, and it balances out nicely with the other frequencies. The midrange is very present and natural sounding judging by how vocals and guitar strings sound. The highs are beautiful, they sound very accurate to me and present no sibilance. The overall sound is very rich and detailed, it allows you to follow specific instruments as you listen, and it even presents some soundstage (which I didn't think was possible in in-ears, maybe my aforementioned B&O H3 had some)

Overall these do have a V sound signature with boosted bass and treble, but not as marked as almost everything else that's in the market. In order to eliminate any fatigue caused by this, I would strongly recommend that you disable any bass boost, make sure you're not elevating bass or treble at all in EQ, and go even deeper and disable default features like Dolby Atmos (Oneplus phone) and even the Hi Fi quad DAC on LG phones (which I've found does introduce a bit of a V curve itself)

Other than their sound these earphones' build quality seems very good and durable. I'm in disbelief they could cost $60. You're welcome
text_fidelity_b: KZ ZS10 Pro, Linsoul 4BA+1DD 5 Driver in Ear Monitor, HiFi Metal Earphones, with Stainless Steel Faceplate, 2 Pin Detachable Cable (Without Mic, Black)

text_fidelity_a:
PIONEER Truly Wireless in-Ear Headphones, Black, SE-C8TW(B) If you're an iphone user, you're probably wondering whether to buy these Pioneer wireless headphones or the Apple version. The Pioneer price is about 1/3 cheaper than Apple. The Pioneer earbuds fit in your ear, so you get much better sound and much better sound isolation. These are nowhere near as detailed or loud as similarly priced wired headphones, but that's true of all wireless Bluetooth earbuds. I will say the connection is stable and not noisy, so these are better than most cheap Bluetooth earbuds. There is some bass, but don't work well for bass-heavy music. Maximum volume is just OK. Battery life is only about 3 hours per charge (compared to 5 hours for Apple), then you have to put the earbuds back in the case for a 1 hour charge. 3 hours may be enough for you; you have to decide, but 5 hours is certainly going to be more interesting to most people. The charging case is much larger than the Apple charging case. The case is 3.3 inches long and 2.2 inches wide. These case is to big to fit comfortably in my pants pocket, so I would only carry it with me in a backpack or purse.

Usage is pretty simple. They paired easily with my phone as a normal Bluetooth device. The buttons on the headphones are easy to use. They are comfortable in my ears. They are secure enough so far, never feeling like they are going to fall out. They are not noticeably heavy like some earbuds can be. When in my ears, they are much less ugly than the Apple earbuds.

I would give these 5 stars for the price and performance if the sound and battery life were better. Frankly, I've tried a few different totally wireless earbuds and been less than impressed by all of them. Bluetooth headphones that have a wire connecting the two pieces can be had for much lower prices and have much better sound quality and much better battery life. Removing the wire just doesn't seem worth the downsides to me.
text_fidelity_b: PIONEER Truly Wireless in-Ear Headphones, Black, SE-C8TW(B)

text_fidelity_a:
Amazon Basics Microphone for Smartphones with Clip - Black This microphone includes a smartphone clip stand. It works fine with my Pixel 2 phone when I connect it to the USB-C dongle cable that was included with my phone. Audio quality is better than phone's built-in microphone, but not as good as the more expensive Shure, Sennheiser, or Audio-Technica microphones that I have used. For voice recording, this microphone is adequate, but for live music performances, I recommend something better. One big advantage of an external microphone is you can aim it at the sound source, instead of relying on whatever direction your phone's microphone is pointing when you aim the camera.

There are a lot of cheap off-brand lavalier microphones on Amazon that work adequately for voice recording, especially at close range. Very hard for me to tell if this one is significantly better than the $10 products.
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Basics Microphone for Smartphones with Clip - Black

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech for Creators Blue Yeti X Professional USB Condenser Microphone for PC, Mac,Gaming,Recording, Streaming, Podcasting on PC, Desktop Mic High-Res Metering, LED Lighting,Blue VO!CE Effects-Black This is a fancier version of the popular Blue Yeti amateur-quality USB microphone with a much higher price tag ($170 vs $110). For the extra money, you get 4 condensers (instead of 3) to give you higher-resolution 24-bit audio (instead of 16-bit) plus a bunch of fancier control and display options. The new microphone has the same directional recording patterns to isolate the recording to your intended audio sources. Is the new microphone worth the extra money? If you really need 24-bit audio, then definitely yes. If not, the new display and control features are more convenient than a huge jump in functionality. The Blue Yeti is still a great microphone for amateur USB recording (podcasts, musical performances, etc). The new version is a step forward, but not worth the price for everyone.

My biggest complaint is that the new microphone uses the same ancient mini-USB interface as the old one. Modern ultralight laptops are moving to the USB-C standard and mini-USB is 2 generations old. You could use a USB-C hub to give you a mini-USB interface, but I wish all modern devices came with USB-C ports since this has been the standard for the last few years.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech for Creators Blue Yeti X Professional USB Condenser Microphone for PC, Mac,Gaming,Recording, Streaming, Podcasting on PC, Desktop Mic High-Res Metering, LED Lighting,Blue VO!CE Effects-Black

2. I had read that Kindle Fire owners were able to use a Nook app, but I found that the app does not work on this newer model.
3. I don't like being limited to apps from Amazon - I couldn't even get mobile banking apps for the 2 major banks that I use.

text_fidelity_a:
ASUS ZenBook 13 Ultra-Slim Laptop, 13.3” Full HD WideView, 8th Gen Intel Core i5-8265U, 8GB LPDDR3, 512GB PCIe SSD, Backlit KB, Fingerprint, Slate Gray, Windows 10, UX331FA-AS51 This review is about what I think >90% of users will care about. The detail specs are a step further, higher and faster and advertised and advertised. The Asus ZenBook 13 has been my go-to everyday toting computer for some 7-8 years.

I have last year’s i5 gen7 ZenBook 13 to directly compare the two.

P.S. This Zen-book has been so good that I had it modified to incorpoarte medical practice compliant HIPA secured software. It's a step function increase in my nightly homework replacing my 7-year old Dell. This laptop is ubiquitously practical with 180 screen twist for descirbing patient procedures. With the med-system handshacks, its like 3x faster than the Dell.

First, this new i5 gen8 ZenBook 13 has a quarter inch all-around smaller footprint. The 1/4" is immediately noticeable from last year’s edition. The 1/4" bezel is noticeably better. As small a footprint as the two have, Asus has reduced the size with no compromise in keyboard utility.

This year's ZenBook is noticeably thinner. Recharge and headphone jack are reversed. This year's hinge is slightly more robust to account for the reduced thickness. The hinge has been a 'should improve' on ZenBooks since inception. This years may solve the issue for good.

The plug-outs are changed. Make sure the output ports are what you want. For my purposes, the addition of a standard HDMI vice last year’s mini-HDMI is an improvement requiring no adapter. Last year’s SD input has been correctly reduced to the increasingly popular/common micro-SD. Plug-out needs are easily resolved with a USB-C adapter hub.

The discrete Nvidia graphics will be an interesting exploration.

The Asus fingerprint reader has never failed. This edition looks identical to last years and has been creatively moved right and off the touchpad. The ZenBook has been the very best reader compared to my HP Envy (dang good) and Dell XPS (50:50 chance).

This year's battery is new tech. The lithium-polymer battery promises up to 14 hours and includes fast-charge technology that takes "just 49 minutes" to recharge to 60% capacity. I get 11 hours out of last year’s battery every day. I can't recall running out of battery on last years on battery save mode on trans-con flights.

Wish it came with Windows Pro instead of Home, but oh well.

Finally, both last years and this year are so fast you'd have to instrument to tell a speed difference. The ZenBooks 1-2-3 second boot to Windows is 'instant' for practical purposes.

Love it. Exceeds expectations. There's no purchase mistake to be made with the UX331.
text_fidelity_b: ASUS ZenBook 13 Ultra-Slim Laptop, 13.3” Full HD WideView, 8th Gen Intel Core i5-8265U, 8GB LPDDR3, 512GB PCIe SSD, Backlit KB, Fingerprint, Slate Gray, Windows 10, UX331FA-AS51

text_fidelity_a:
Arctic Cooling P311-BK Bluetooth Stereo Headset with Microphone Overall, these are a decent pair of bluetooth earphones. The build quality is good for the price, with sturdy arms that fold so the headphones can be stowed easily in a carry case (or pocket). The ear padding is on the thin side, but there's enough to maintain comfort for a reasonable amount of wear time.

The sound quality is more than decent for the price. They won't stun you with huge bass and crisp mid and upper ranges, but for general all-purpose listening (e.g., music, movies, etc.) they get the job done well.

It paired easily with a Fire and a Nexus. The operating range is quite good - I had no problems maintaining a connection from the opposite side of a large room (about 20 or so feet).

Misses center on two issues: controls and the case. The controls are small and unobtrusive, which is nice from an aesthetic standpoint - the headset casing looks sleek. However, in actual usage, it can be hard to find the proper button by touch alone. Some type of tactile cue would have been nice to ensure you get to the right button each and every time.

I also think the case could have been better. While it's stylish (sort of a triangular shape) with a crease in the cover that adds visual interest, there's no mesh or straps on the inside to hold the headphones and/or cables. The end result is that while the case looks nicer than others I've used, it's not as practical or functional. I find that to be a significant issue since I use these type of headphones away from home (e.g., at the gym, while exercising, etc.) and the carry case gets used a lot.

Given that these are priced the same or a bit higher than other similar bluetooth headsets, these misses warrant dropping the rating by one star. However, they remain a good choice if you're looking for a generally inexpensive set of headphones - they sound pretty good, seems to be well-made, and have a good operating range.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Arctic Cooling P311-BK Bluetooth Stereo Headset with Microphone

text_fidelity_a:
Canon EF 100mm f/2.8 Macro USM Fixed Lens for Canon SLR Cameras Although this lens is intended for macro photography, it's also a great lens for general purpose shots, or portrait shots. The lens produces beautiful sharp images and is a fast, accurate focuser. The lens is moderately heavy and bulky, so I wouldn't classify it as eminently carryable, and without image stabilization, you might suffer hand shake blur if you're not shooting at the wide end; at smaller apertures, using it with a tripod is highly recommended. But if you're buying it primarily to get into macro this shouldn't much matter as tripod shooting with macro is virtually a necessity, and completely expected.

The 100mm focal length is a nice compromise when you want to get close to small subjects (particularly insects) but are limited to how close you can get before scaring the subject off - as a comparison with the 180mm macro, you would want to factor in a consideration as to what you might like to shoot most of the time - big spiders that you'd rather stay well away from might be an application more suited to the 180mm, for instance, but if you are keen to shoot mostly flowers, the 180 might be more length than you really need.

In short, the 100mm macro is one of my "keeper" lenses, a real performer.
text_fidelity_b: Canon EF 100mm f/2.8 Macro USM Fixed Lens for Canon SLR Cameras

text_fidelity_a:
Sony UBP-X800 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray Player Picture is nice,

The real reason I'm sending the units (I've had two) back, however, is that the player refuses to output the various high quality audio formats, including 7.1 DTS Master Audio. The digital coax cable barely works and the HDMI 2 audio output simply does not work, Admittedly I have an older receiver -- a Sony STR-DA5400ES, from 2009. But it has multiple HDMI inputs and the HDMI 2 audio output on the X800 is specifically designed to send audio to an older amp. Even Sony phone support says it should work. But it doesn't.. I spent 1 hour and 7 minutes with Sony ES support today going through every possible menu permutation on both the Amp and the UBP-X800 player. No luck The HDMI is dead. Zero output. The coax output can only send DTS EX 5.1, even though the player itself tells me it's playing DTS Master Audio 7.1.

This UBP-X800 has two HDMI outputs: one for video, one for audio. In case you don't have a 4K receiver with the ever-changing HDMI protocols, you're supposed to be able to feed HDMI audio to the amp. So I fed the video directly to the Samsung's video input (a direct cable connection) and another HDMI to my amp.

Zero audio from the player's HDMI audio feed. Not a peep of audio at all.

So I used the orange RCA digital audio coax connector to get surround sound audio.

But the coax digital audio cable only delivers DTS EX 5.1, not the 7.1 DTS Master Audio available on the Kingsman 4K disk. I updated the player's and the TV's firmware and read the manual. Nothing fixes the problem. Using all new, very short, high-speed HDMI 2.0 cables too.

My ancient Sony BDP-S560 Blu-ray player feeds all formats to the same 5400ES amp properly. I get great 7.1 DTS Master HD audio. Thus my old Blu-ray player sounds way better than my brand new advanced Sony UHD player.
Researching at the Sony forum under the UBP-X800 Audio Problems thread, answers were all over the place and none worked, I tried to register so I could post my problem and the website wouldn't allow me to. The comments there were complaining that they could not get the ATMOS tracks working.

I have no choice but to pack both X800s up and send them back.

Eventually I found that I needed to plug the 4K player into input 3 of the TV for the image to stabilize. Interesting that only some inputs on the TV can handle UHD source. But still, the player's audio doesn't work with my Sony Amp (Sony's fault).

HDMI was supposed to solve all these problems, but I suspect the HDCP copy protection schemes are really screwing things up or the firmware has bugs or companies just produce inferior products. Rather disappointing.
text_fidelity_b: Sony UBP-X800 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray Player

Antennas Direct ClearStream 1MAX HDTV Antenna UHF VHF, Multi-Directional, 40+ Mile Range, UHD 4K, NEXTGEN TV – w/Adjustable Mounting Hardware (Black) Trying to decide if we were ready to cut the cord, we installed this antenna to see if we could get all the local channels. We got 40 digital channels about 20 miles west of Washington DC and the major networks are crystal clear.

The network towers we use are clustered together about 20 miles away. We have 2 or more topographical obstructions between our house and the towers (no line of sight). The Noise Margin on the networks is 35-40 dB. TVFool.com listed my location as "yellow" (which means use an attic antenna or higher). The cable drop is about 25 feet and I did not use an amplifier.

This antenna is supposed to be omni-directional but we did experience occasional signal drop on the networks with the initial "eyeball" installation (which was off about 15 degrees). Standing directly under the antenna and looking through a compass I had my son walk through the yard until he stepped into the path to the towers. Then I had him stand still, facing the antenna, and rotated it until he told me it was pointed straight over his head. That seemed to fix the signal drops. Given all the factors of our situation, I am probably maxing out the performance of this antenna. If I have any issues I'll just buy the add-on the reflector shield to increase directional performance...but for right now I don't need it.

Installation was easy (I just mounted it to the Direct TV mast). This antenna is small and light which was a big plus when climbing up a 25 foot ladder.

So far so good!
text_fidelity_b: Antennas Direct ClearStream 1MAX HDTV Antenna UHF VHF, Multi-Directional, 40+ Mile Range, UHD 4K, NEXTGEN TV – w/Adjustable Mounting Hardware (Black)

HP Wireless Elite Keyboard v2 ...if you don't have a wrist rest or pad already, I highly recommend that you get one at the same time you get this keyboard. I was introduced to the chiclet- or scissor-style keyboard because of using one at work (using an Apple wired keyboard with an Intel Mac), and I have to say that I prefer it in every way to the more traditional keyboards. It is much quieter, and, for me, the feedback is pleasant. One thing I did not take into account, though, is that I had a wrist rest at work. Overall, this is a great keyboard. For reasons I will not go into here, I am using this keyboard with a laptop: the laptop keyboard's lights indicate whether or not I have Caps Lock or Num Lock engaged on the wireless keyboard. I understand that won't help people using this keyboard with a desktop computer, but thought I'd put it out there anyway.

My conclusion: if you're a fan of the scissor-style keyboard and you have or are willing to invest in a wrist rest, you will enjoy this keyboard.

And many of our devices don't come with built-in CD/DVD drives these days, since flash drives and cloud storage and downloadable software and streaming video have pretty much taken the load for now.

But some of us still have DVD movie collections and still have an occasional need for a CD/DVD drive. And this is a good one.

It's USB powered and doesn't need an extra power adapter. It comes with two USB cables --- both USB type A (the regular kind) and type C (the newer reversible kind).

Here are a few of the specs:

Read/write speed is 8X for DVDs and 24X for CDs, 4X for DVD video playback.
USB interface is 2.0 (not 3.0).
It's compatible with Window 10, 8, 7, Vista, and XP, and Mac OS X 10.6 and above.
It has M-disc support.

It comes with bundled software for backing up and encryption that you may or may not want to use.

Western Digital 320GB WD Black Performance Mobile Hard Drive - 7200 RPM Class, SATA 6 Gb/s, , 32 MB Cache, 2.5" - WD3200LPLX Update 8-7-19: I went to the WD website to register my two drives. They show as no warranty from WD, presumably because they were bought through a reseller. Just so you know ...

I use these as primary storage (and backup storage) for our MacBook Air laptop. Most MacBooks now come with solid state drives, meaning memory chip based drives, not physical spinning disks. They are much more expensive than the heritage physical disk approach, such that the largest SSD that we could get with our 2017 MacBook Air was a 256 GB drive. These WD Black (virtually enterprise level) drives are 500 GB each, so our storage is 2x that of the built in drive. We use one as our primary external drive; once a month we install the 2nd drive (also externally), copy the files across, and put it into our safe deposit box at the bank. If we ever lose a drive, whether to failure or someone breaking in and stealing our drive and laptop, we're only 30 days behind, a real advantage.

The only downside to this drive is that the warranty on the drive itself is provided by the Seller, OEMGENUINE. The drive came marked with a label on the drive as a Seller 5 year warranty, with no terms provided. The downside risk is there is no published warranty, either by the Seller or by WD on their website, and whatever warranty is provided is subject to the Seller still being in existence over the next 5 years. However, given the price of the drive ($35 or so), it was a reasonable risk to take, especially since we acquired two and use one as the backup to the primary one. The odds of losing two drives at the same time is pretty remote. So we accepted the risk, but dropped the review for the product & seller by 1 star. If you go to the WD website, they do claim a 5 year limited warranty. I am a little surprised that the WD website doesn't provide a link to their warranty. So if we can't reach OEMGENUINE should we have a problem, I'm not sure what protection we'll have from WD. Something to consider if that's important to you.

These are fast drives (7200 rpm for the 500GB drive), which is noticeably faster than the previous bulk drives we've purchased online and/or removed from existing systems, which have all been 5400 rpm drives. SATA compatible, plug and play, no issues yet but it's only been a few days. If something materially changes, I'll post an update.
text_fidelity_b: Western Digital 320GB WD Black Performance Mobile Hard Drive - 7200 RPM Class, SATA 6 Gb/s, , 32 MB Cache, 2.5" - WD3200LPLX

text_fidelity_a:
BRAINWAVZ S0 in-Ear Earbuds Noise Isolating Earphones Clearwavz Remote & Microphone Stereo Headphone Headset for iPhone iPad, iPod & Android Devices (Black) I love how comfortable these ear buds are. I’ve always been pleased with Brainwavz earphone comfort, but these have raised the comfort bar even higher. I’m using it mainly with the tri-flange tips which I’ve tried with other headphones but didn't care that much for. With the S0's, however, the tri-flange fit very well, provide for good sound isolation, and stay put even when I’m on the treadmill. Very well done.

The sound quality is also quite pleasing. There’s ample bass without it being boomy or muddy. Just a nice, solid low-frequency response that sounds great. The mid-range is clear even at higher volumes. The only small shortfall is with the upper ranges, which are not as clear and sharp as they could be, and get somewhat shrill at high volumes. But at normal volumes it’s a nicely balanced sound, and considering the price, I would describe the sound quality as very good overall.

The build quality feels pretty solid. The cables are well-attached and have molded connectors at the ear buds to give it better durability. That’s important for me since, while this comes with a very nice carry case, I usually just wrap the cords around whatever device I’m using, which puts a lot of stress on the connectors. These feel more than solid enough to deal with that level of abuse. I have a few other Brainwavz earphones and have yet to have one fail on me.

This is well worth a spot on your short list if you’re shopping for a well-made, comfortable set of earbuds that deliver solid sound without breaking the bank. Highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: BRAINWAVZ S0 in-Ear Earbuds Noise Isolating Earphones Clearwavz Remote & Microphone Stereo Headphone Headset for iPhone iPad, iPod & Android Devices (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Sony RX100 IV 20.1 MP Premium Compact Digital Camera w/ 1-inch Sensor, 4K Movies and 40x Super Slow Motion HD DSCRX100M4/B Black I've said it a thousand times: "I think I could really get into (real) photography, but I just can't take another hobby that requires me carrying a whole bag of equipment across the world. If I get a DSLR, I won't take it to the places that I'd like to use it the most." Well...I think they made this camera just for me. I believe this camera to be capable of "real" pro photos, just the same as if I bought a DSLR and a single lens, which many people start by doing. It also makes a startup punk like me look like a pro, much to the chagrin of the real pros.

My other cameras include a DSC-H20, which is an older Sony model with a 10x zoom lens, multiple point-and-shoots, and a waterproof/shockproof Panasonic that I really like for my basic, worry-free shots.

My main question about this camera was, why does it appear to be Sony's flagship compact camera in every way, but yet it doesn't have the 30x optical zoom lens that some of the other Sony's have (or even the 10x of my DSC-H20)? I knew there would be an answer, but to find it, I had to start digging into camera specs, something I've been meaning to do for a while.

First, pro photographers tend to think that if you're using much zoom under most circumstances, then you're just being lazy. You need to get closer. In a landscape shot, zoom tends to flatten things out. I may have never noticed this, or WHY this is. You know, you go on vacation, take a lot of pictures, come back and some look great and others look bad. Maybe it's true that every time I zoom in on a landscape, I'm really just ruining my shot.

The other thing is aperture. Aperture basically tells you how clear the background of your picture will be versus your foreground (I'm just learning this myself, so camera pros, feel free to comment with better verbiage), a lower number being better if you want a totally clear picture, and the lowness of that number being what you use to compare the quality of lenses. It's also good to have a high end on the range because that allows you to take those artsy photos with something super clean up front and a blurry background. I've also seen some neat head shots taken that way, where even some hair starts becoming blurry.

Anyway, the low aperture on this camera is 1.8 all the way zoomed out, and 2.8 all the way zoomed in (you can set it as high as 11 in either case). This is a tight range with great numbers (notice that even here, you lose a little bit by using zoom). My camera with the 10x zoom has an aperture equal to 3.5 all the way out, similar to the 30x zoom cameras Sony has now. It makes a big difference, even to my amateur eye.

This camera, and my subsequent research, has allowed me to let go of the 10/30x zoom. Yes, those cameras are great, but this is the flagship mini for a reason. Now I understand. Just taking random pictures in my neighborhood, although so boring compared to my favorite International backgrounds, I can clearly see a quality difference.

The other main spec for cameras is shutter speed. This can be set for 1/32000 of a second all the way up to 30 seconds. The quickest shutter speeds will capture an instant in time without blur, while the slower ones will capture more action with some blur. They are also good for low light scenarios to expose the shot to more light. Very slow speeds should be used with a tripod or the camera set down someplace. This camera makes a noise (not an obnoxious one) when on auto and using a slower shutter speed, to keep you still. It's very intuitive and works well.

While you will get better shots than you ever had before using this camera on auto, the dial wheel allows you to set either aperture or shutter speed as a priority and leave the rest on auto, perfect for people that want to understand what a real camera can do, and who want to set up pro shots without yet knowing everything.

The controls on this thing are awesome. I love that there is no touchscreen to fight with and that everything is so intuitive. Great praise to Sony for knowing what fads aren't worth it. (One fad they did latch onto is that 180 degree rotating screen, which really is fantastically convenient and feels quite strong and well done). While we're talking about it, they also put in the fantastic viewfinder and the pop-up flash, which all completely recess into the body of this thing (an amazing work of engineering art).

Speaking of the flash, you won't use it often. Even on a cheap camera, I try to keep the flash off, but this thing does an amazing job of using ambient light for exposure (I believe this is the third pillar of photography). I swear, I have never seen such clear pictures in very low light. Instead of being grainy, I can pick up minute details (even zoom-able), and they appear brighter than the actual place they were taken. This, I believe, is because of the 1" image sensor they are touting. I'm impressed.

The 960fps thing. With only two seconds, this may be hard to set up the shot you want, but 2 seconds seems a lot longer in 960fps. Even just shaking your leg on camera, you'll see the odd aftereffects of your socks moving like you never did before. Stupid example, but that's the point: the details you get from 960fps slow-mo are amazing.

4k video. I really didn't care about all this until some guy at a conference pointed out how 4k has been used for pro video for years. Instead of multiple cameras to cover a hockey game, for example, you could just use one and zoom in on anything you want and still have high-def video. I realized we probably will move over to actually using it at some point. Well, here's your chance to actually use that 4k TV. It's awesome. It really is.

A note on SD cards. While most devices can read SDHC cards, which went up to 32GB, the reason they want you to have a SDXC card (which can be from 64GB to 2TB in theory) is because the speed ratings are higher. You need the speed rating of 3 (>100 Mbps) to really use these big data transfer functions. I suspect the 960fps is all that can be held in RAM, and that those speeds are way too fast for even the newest and best card (hence the 2 second limit on 960fps).

Suffice to say that I love this camera. I appreciate each of its mechanical and electrical features and how they're perfectly integrated to make this small, marvelous camera. Even in the leather case (not included), it's about the same size as my H20, certainly portable enough to have it when you want it, but with enough features and technology that you're not sacrificing anything in your photography.
text_fidelity_b: Sony RX100 IV 20.1 MP Premium Compact Digital Camera w/ 1-inch Sensor, 4K Movies and 40x Super Slow Motion HD DSCRX100M4/B Black

Zip Ties 8 inch (1000 Pack), 40lbs Tensile Strength, Black Cable Ties, Wire Ties for indoor and outdoor use, by Skalon When it comes to zip ties; they either do what they're supposed to, or they don't. If you are simply expecting these to hold things together reasonably well, then they are perfectly adequate for the task. However, when I tested them by tying them to weights and using them to lift, I found that they broke about 1/2 the time at 30 pounds, never quite reaching 40 pounds.

They are reliably good for 20 pounds without breaking, which is not too bad, really, for something so small. While I feel that the 40 pound claim is somewhat misleading, they are actually comparable to most similar sized ties on the market as far as I can tell, and it's doubtful that most others would perform any better. If you're not using them to lift heavy weights then they'll work just fine, and you'd be hard pressed to find a better price for this quantity of similar ties.

text_fidelity_a:
WiFi Extender Long Range Repeater 300Mbps Router Wireless Access Point Signal Amplifier Booster Complies with 802.11n/g/b with WPS Button,Extends WiFi to Smart Home & Alexa Devices Just got this today because we are having wifi accessibility issues in our upstairs guest bedroom (and every good host knows that if you don't have decent wifi in your guest room, you can expect your guests to leave you a holy mess, in retaliation).

Couldn't believe how easy this is to set up, though! I'm pretty tech-savvy, anyhow (after 2 years of various tech-related military schools). Not that I needed to be! The included instructions are incredibly clear and easy to follow. On the contrary, the last AP/repeater I bought merely schooled me in when it's acceptable to take a hammer to one of these things. (FYI: it's right after you've tried, unsuccessfully, for an hour to get it to connect to your wifi). So I really appreciated how simple and fast this is to set up.

How fast, exactly? It literally took like 2 minutes to set up...and only THAT long because I had to go all the way into the other room and log into my laptop to complete the instructions.

Just a head's up, for the less-tech savvy:

This is NOT a wifi signal amplifier, as such. You WILL be creating a NEW wireless access point (aka wifi log-on)...even if you install this in "repeater" mode--vs. the wired-to-wireless AP (access point) mode.

So, for example, instead of logging into whatever your network is called, when you need to use the wifi that this repeats for you, you'll be logging into a new connection. They call it, by default, "My Repeater" (I assume that is so you'll never forget who actually owns it), but you can rename it to anything you want (mine is henceforth known as Fluffy Gigglebuns). You'll still use the same password as you use for your main connection, though...and therein lies the genius of it. You can make your guests feel special (or, in my case, humiliated) by personalizing the repeater network name, but the password will be the same as it is for whatever network AP you are having it repeat.

Lastly, this does offer an extra feature I think is worth mentioning:

You can also use this as a wireless adapter to connect a multimedia or other tech device that requires or ONLY allows internet connectivity via an ethernet (aka wired) connection.

ASUS C201PA-DS02 11.6-Inch Laptop (Navy Blue) This is my first time using a Chromebook and I didn't know what to expect. I mean it's sort of like a laptop in size but it runs on Chrome, not Windows.

Start-up was fast, almost super fast. You open the cover and BAM, within seconds, you're online. Very cool.

The display is HD and very crisp. I viewed a couple of Netflix nature movies and the display was stunning. No lag or fuzziness. There's a Micro HDMI so you can view on a big screen, but a cable is not included.

The wi-fi is dual-band 802.11 and is fast as well. I had no issues connecting at home, work, or the local coffee shop.

There is 16gb of local storage, but Google includes 100gb of Google Drive storage for 2 years. Personally I've never used more than 3gb of storage, so 100gb should be adequate for most people.

The internal speakers weren't great, but they didn't suck either. Sound was crisp but slightly muted. A pair of USB speakers took care of this. Soon I was rocking in the coffee shop (i forgot my headphones).

Because of my big fingers I'm not a fan of the pad thingy. I was able to plug in a bluetooth mouse and was up and running within 30 seconds. At first I wasn't sure if the Chromebook would allow peripherals, but it did with no issues.

The battery is stated to last 13 hours. I haven't gone that far yet, but I've gotten a solid 5 hours of mixed internet/video streaming use and still had 50% battery left.

The fit and finish is top notch although the top cover can be a finger print magnet. I just throw a microfiber cloth in my bag.

The keyboard has ample sized 'chicklet' keys which are soft and silent. My big fingers had no issues hitting other keys by accident.

In closing, I'm a convert!

My laptops were mainly used for the internet and watching movies. With everything online, like Netflix, Hulu, and Prime movies, this Chromebook rocks!
text_fidelity_b: ASUS C201PA-DS02 11.6-Inch Laptop (Navy Blue)

text_fidelity_a:
SK hynix Gold S31 1TB SATA Gen3 2.5 inch Internal SSD | SSD 1TB | Up to 560MB/S | Solid State Drive | Compact 2.5" SSD Form Factor SSD | Internal Solid State Drive | SATA SSD Revving up old Macs is like one of my favorite things. I don't do much of it anymore, because (a) arthritis in my hands has made the turning of tiny screws much more of a chore, and (b) I was running out of old Macs.

The last one I had was a 2010 mini that was the first computer I'd bought new since probably 1993 (also a Mac). It had the last of the Core2Duo processors and a spin up hard drive and a couple of gigs of ram that I upgraded pretty much right away. It served as a DVR for a while, then a minecraft server, media streamer, then got put away. I resurrected it to bounce DATS to .WAV to mp3 when I learned that it had digital audio input and output. I had been researching all these expensive things to make that happen, and it turned out that my little friend was able to save me hundreds of dollars with something that had been built in all along.

But it was slow because of the HDD. And upgrading looked really daunting. I'd done one of the earlier minis, and it had been an exercise in anxiety.

But the other day, I decided to give it a try. Two bits of advice: if you can get through this without disconnecting the wifi connector (you can if you are really careful), do so, and (2) if you accidentally disconnect the wifi connector (I did), don't panic. Watch videos of people putting iPhones back together (the older, the better). These connectors are fussy. Do not force them. If they are seated correctly, a light press will connect them. You'll feel the click. But it's almost like threading a needle to get it seated correctly. And if you push too hard, you'll break it. Same with the fan. Just be careful. If you are pushing and it's not connecting right away, it's not lined up right.

Okay, so deciding to do the drive replacement took awhile because the above two steps seemed very daunting. And the project took me several hours, because I had to stop and rest a few times (if your hands work and you keep your screws organized, it should take about 45 minutes). But it was worth every minute.

This is an excellent drive. The form factor lines up exactly with the HDD I pulled from the mini (some of the drives I have used in old white MacBooks and older MacBook Pros have not). Not a millimeter off. The OS install flew. This drive is stellar in this context. If you need a 2.5" SSD, I highly recommend this one.
text_fidelity_b: SK hynix Gold S31 1TB SATA Gen3 2.5 inch Internal SSD | SSD 1TB | Up to 560MB/S | Solid State Drive | Compact 2.5" SSD Form Factor SSD | Internal Solid State Drive | SATA SSD

I usually prefer over-ear headphones because they are more comfortable for me -- I have quite a few inner ear piercings -- but I’ve barely used any other set of headphones for the past month.

Once you find the right size, these buds are comfortable and stay in your ears. The box includes three sizes of ear tips: small, medium, and large. I did have a short adjustment period, the noise cancelling made me nauseated. This is not a fault of the earbuds, it’s something that can happen, and within a week, I was able to wear the earbuds for hours at a time.

I use the earbuds to listen to music and stream shows. I’m not an audiophile, but I think the sound quality is pretty good. Music sounds clear and punchy, no tin can or thin bass here. The noise cancelling is not as robust as a pair of over-ear headphones, but it dampens enough of the background noise in my home that I can clearly hear what I have playing.

The main advantage of these earbuds is they don’t give me a headache like over-ear ones do after a few hours. There’s no headband sitting on top of my head, or squeezy tight ear cups. As I mentioned, I have a few inner ear piercings (tragus, rook, daith) and I’m still able to wear the earbuds comfortably. They stay in while I walk around the house.

I can use one earbud or both, and they have tap controls. They connect easily, all it takes is opening the case and they’re connected to my computer.

The case is pretty swanky, matte black with a thin strip of metallic red. The case has 4 small LEDs on the front to show battery and charging status, the lights go on when opening the case or when it’s charging. The case works with wireless charging or via USB-C, a short cable is included.

The wheel is by far my biggest issue with this mouse.

text_fidelity_a:
Bose CineMate 1 SR Home Theater Speaker System (Black) I bought this system to replace my Yamaha YSP-500 and a fairly sizeable subwoofer. My issue was that we were doing a remodel of our living room to put in a wall with a fireplace and stonework where our existing entertainment center was. Because the Yamaha projector is fairly substantial, mounting it directly to the wall wasn't an option, so I would have had to build another shelf or do something else. I would have also had to relocate the sub which would have meant either buying some sort of wireless set up or running a cable under the floor and into the wall.

Since the Bose speaker is much slimmer and lighter, has an available wall bracket, and the sub is wireless I thought I had the solution to my problem. For that part, the Bose is great. It was easy to mount, is relatively unobtrusive, and having more flexibility with the placement of the sub is really nice. If you have space limitations or just don't want to mess with running speaker wire (or can't) then this is a good alternative.

This is also a good alternative for people that just want to plug something in and have it work. If you are technically challenged, or just don't want to invest the time in setting up a home theater then this is a usable solution. Most people could have this up and running (including configuration) in less than 20 minutes.

I thought the sound quality is pretty decent. I don't know that it is significantly better than the older (and cheaper) Yamaha Sound Projector that it replaced. Unlike some reviewers, I thought voices (at least on television shows) were clearer and easier to hear than what I was used to. The bass was crisp, but I haven't experienced the punch I am used to with my Yamaha sub. Granted the Bose Accoustimass module is a lot smaller, but there is a very noticeable difference.

There are two areas that I took a star away for each. One is obviously cost. At around $1000, I would say that this would be a better value. At its current price I think that you are not really getting what you pay for. For all the trade-offs, I think there are cheaper alternatives.

The second is the fact that it lacks any sort of display or ability to customize. You can't make any sort of sound profiles (movies, sports, etc), you don't have anything like a night mode, and there is no display whatsoever to indicate something as simple as volume level. Some people may like that, but to me it was rather annoying. For the price, I think you should be able to do a little more with it. Again, if you are the plug-and-play type, this probably won't bother you.

Overall, other than the size and wireless sub, this is not an improvement from my Yamaha Sound Projector. I think it's good, but if I had to do it over again I would probably look at other, cheaper options.
text_fidelity_b: Bose CineMate 1 SR Home Theater Speaker System (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Alphasonik ASE300BT Bluetooth Headphones, V4.0 Wireless Sport Headphones, Sweatproof Running Headset with Built in Mic for Workout Exercise IPX5 SplashProof, Ergonomically Designed for Extra Comfort I do a LOT of work in front of a computer, and was getting these for when I work at home. At work, I use a Logitech 930 headset that I really like. I got these so I wouldn't yank my laptop off the desk when I get up. I got bluetooth, thinking they'd be easy to sync to my various devices. So, here's my breakdown:

Range
I can go upstairs and grab a few things or go two rooms away and I still get a signal. The range is pretty good on these.

Playback Sound
The playback sound quality is okay. Not blowing me away, but alright. I listen to music, no vocals, to block out the office noise and keep my head focused. The playback audio goes into tin-can mode when the mic is enabled. That's something I didn't realize as a limitation of how bluetooth handles the two signals. That took me a while to figure out.

Microphone
The mic is okay. It just flips me out that the playback goes into "phone mode" when the mic is enabled.

Battery
Well, I've only had these a couple of months. But, the battery seems to go at least as long as I can stand to keep them on my head. Max has been about 2 hours at a stretch before giving my head/ears a break.

Fit
I'm an adult and my head is average-sized, not large. After maybe three months these cans are still a bit tight. The cups don't quite fit entirely over my ears and get uncomfortable after maybe two hours --like, *ouch* uncomfortable.

Heat
These cans get pretty hot after maybe 45 minutes. Hot like I just got out of the shower and I need a towel in my ears hot. I don't think I've ever had sweaty ears like this before from a set of headphones.

Sync
I've easily sync'd these to Ubuntu 14.04 & 10, Windows 7, and OS X Mavericks.

Would I recommend these to a friend?
No. I like not having to carry a dongle around since bluetooth is in all of my computers (one has an $8 dongle that works just fine.) But, they get so hot, and are still not comfortable on my head and ears after maybe 100 hours of use. So, for the $50 price tag, I'd probably have to say no. If they were $25 and just to make the occasional phone call I might recommend them to a friend, but not to wear for any period of time. If they were just a bit more comfortable, and breathed a bit better, I'd change my mind. Maybe in the next revision, Photive?
text_fidelity_b: Alphasonik ASE300BT Bluetooth Headphones, V4.0 Wireless Sport Headphones, Sweatproof Running Headset with Built in Mic for Workout Exercise IPX5 SplashProof, Ergonomically Designed for Extra Comfort

text_fidelity_a:
Arlo VMS5140-100NAS Ultra - 4K UHD Wire-Free Security 1 Camera System Update: one star. Stopped holding a charge after 3 months.

These are the first security cameras we've ever used, and I was able to install them myself in about a half hour. While they do a good job recording video and saving it so I can view it on my phone, the app is lacking and there are a couple of things that I find frustrating. I'll break my review into pros and cons.

Pros:
1. Fast install
2. Rechargeable (but only one base station)
3. Can view what is going on in my house when I am not there, can talk to the dog if I see him getting into the trash
4. Backs up my videos so I can look at them later if I am not home but cannot check the notification
5. I like the option to have a light come on at night, sound a siren, or call emergency services.
6. Decent video, I don't think it's 4k HD though, and wonderful audio.

Cons
1. The battery life. It lasts about 5 days, but one of mine is mounted outside so I have to stand on a chair or ladder to disconnect it and reconnect it.
2. Only one charing base is included for two cameras. They usually die around the same time and I can only charge one, the extra chargers are pricey and it seems to be a proprietary wire.
3. It came with one magnetic mount, which I love, and another mount that is a screw and ball. This mount doesn't feel as secure and I don't get why it just didn't have two of the same ones. It looks weird having the same camera with different mounts.
3. They are 4k, IF you pay. If you don't then they record in a lower quality. I don't mind, but it's misleading how it's phrased.
4. The app is clunky. I found it hard to block out areas where I didn't need notifications (like, every car that drives by on the road). I also was overwhelmed with notifications every time someone walks through my living room. I figured out how to set the cameras to a schedule/geo-fence, but WATCH OUT! The geo-fence doesn't work if you disconnect your phone from Wifi when you leave.
5. Notifications: When I'm not home I get an alert every time my cats walk through the room, so I had to shut off notifications all together. A little frustrating, but understandable.
6. Timers. If you want the camera to run from 10pm to 5am, you have to set it for the current day 10pm-11:59 pm, then the next day from 12:01am to 5:00am. It's kind of difficult and it kept not saving it when I set it up that way so I gave up and just set it from 12:01am-5:00am.
text_fidelity_b: Arlo VMS5140-100NAS Ultra - 4K UHD Wire-Free Security 1 Camera System

NETGEAR Cable Modem CM500 - Compatible with all Cable Providers incl. Xfinity, Spectrum, Cox | For Cable Plans up to 400Mbps | DOCSIS 3.0 Comcast has repeatedly lied to me, sending me letters and alerts telling me that I need a new cable modem or my service will be seriously degraded. One time they went so far as to set a date when my service would NO longer work at all! Of course, I would never believe them without double-checking for myself, and I found out it was indeed an outright lie. Even the oldest DOCSIS versions can handle more than my 30Mbps connection. I suppose the lie was because they want me to rent their modem for $10 or more a month and relinquish control of my own network to them.

That said, it makes sense to upgrade when convenient to be sure you're future proofed. Eventually even the cheapest Internet plans will be upgraded to higher speeds. When I heard that I could register this on Comcast's network online without having to call them (and have them speak extremely condescendingly to me even though I'm a Systems Engineer), I was sold. Worth doing.

Note that just because DOCSIS 3.0 can reach speeds of 10Gbps with maxed out number of channels, this modem is 680Mbps, which will be out of date eventually, when we finally get Gigabit Ethernet to residences.

Another (of a million) thing(s) I hate about Comcast is that they by default use your AP (that they rent to you as part of a router/AP/modem combo) to create a public (virtual) wireless AP for their other customers. They say this will not affect your bandwidth, but it can affect your throughput. And it uses your electricity. And why would you want to help Comcast, when they take advantage of you any chance they can.

Point of all this is me encouraging you to get your own modem, get your own router and AP (or combo unit, although I prefer them separate) and pare down your ISP bill as much as you can. Stop giving them money.

Note that apparently if you get voice service through Comcast, you'll still need their combo modem unit of some sort. Well, cut that service from your monthly budget too. If we just had some competition, I'd cut Comcast out of my life completely.

Another thing is that if you have their modem and you need help with it, they may call it your responsibility and charge you for any "help" they provide. At least if you own your own stuff, you'll know if it's your problem or theirs.

Modem is straightforward and easy to use as any. If you ever download at high rates for days on end, it'll need cycled, but that's not the modem's fault; it just happens.
text_fidelity_b: NETGEAR Cable Modem CM500 - Compatible with all Cable Providers incl. Xfinity, Spectrum, Cox | For Cable Plans up to 400Mbps | DOCSIS 3.0

text_fidelity_a:
AGPtEK 16GB Portable MP3 Player(Expandable Up to 128GB), Music Player/Voice Recorder/FM Radio with HD Headphone and Adjustable Sport Armband, M28, Black Software Features:
This AGPtEK mp3 player is a really good alternative to an ipod or zune which is more expensive and offers less storage space while offering the opportunity to drag and drop files into the mp3 player folder directly, once it's connected via usb cable to your computer. This feature is important to me, because not all my music is properly tagged, so music organizing software like itunes doesn't recognise the files. This is no problem with the AGPtEK mp3 player, since I can always manually find the file and drop it in.
Hardware Features: The build is attractive and sturdy. I appreciate the glass display and nice solid but light aluminum casing. The shape is a basic rectangle which works fine for me since I like a minimalist look. One thing I don't like about the build is that the click wheel click very loudly and is a little stiff, which is a hassle to use when you're trying to scroll down your music list.The wheel feels a little cheap, its quality is not on par with the rest of the build. The screen is not as large as a typical ipod's but is sufficient. The title of your song will have to scroll a bit to be read fully, which can be kind annoying. ANother great thing is that you can upgrade storage using a micro SD chip which means you're quadrupling your storage. score!

Music Playback features: They have a nice EQ option if you're into that. The fast forward is really slow. The mp3 player plays a bunch of different formats like mp3, oog, wav, flac, etc... You can also store audiobooks, videos, photos, and record sound. I havn't use these features yet.

Accessories: The arm band is a nice bonus. It fits perfectly and leaves holes for charging and headphones. It holds the mp3 player snuggly. The band is smooth and not scratchy. If you have small arms the band can be pretty big, it's adjustable but there will be somg extra band hanging around. t is fastened by velcro.
The headphones are like $10 quality. They're not bad, but they're not audiophile. They don't fit very well as I have small ears but they'll do in a pinch.

Charging: There is an option to charge and transfer or charge and play music once you connect the player to your computer. CHarging it fully takes about 1-2 hours. The mp3's battery is very good, I haven't been able to drain the battery completely, but keeping it off, it's been able to stay charged for over 3 days.
text_fidelity_b: AGPtEK 16GB Portable MP3 Player(Expandable Up to 128GB), Music Player/Voice Recorder/FM Radio with HD Headphone and Adjustable Sport Armband, M28, Black

text_fidelity_a:
Panasonic SC-BTT195 Energy Star 5.1-Channel 1000-Watt Full HD 3D Blu-Ray Home Theater System with Tall Boy Speakers Good sound for the money and does what I expected. Skip to the summation if you are looking for reasons not to purchase.

Might be a better choice especially if you own a Panasonic TV as the set up is designed for a Panasonic product line. I had to use their support call service a few times and as most companies today, some are very good and can understand and help, but most will read a prewritten script and hope they hit on the problem you are experiencing. Cons: Had to go buy after market speaker wires due to the lack of length that comes with the system and splice the wires to place the rear speakers. Also had to buy an audio connector to allow the system to produce TV sound. This really ticked me off and Panasonic should really step up and correct these issues. The system also needs to modernize and add another HDMI connection ( and the cable ...really? ) to allow for a cleaner install. Another con is the system will not produce sound while watching the Internet based VUDU movie channel. Panasonic wanted me to buy another movie and call them to "try" some fixes while the movie played! It does work with my cable provided paid movie service. The system would also not work with my top of the line wireless router and had to buy a cable and run wires to their system. One must also buy another adapter ( Dingle) to receive wireless signals that may or may not work or a connecting cable. Check to see see the distance from your router to the system and if it is physically possible to fish the wire to the sound system from the router before you buy the cable.

Summation: "You get what you pay for". If you can splice wires and figure out how to add cables to make TV audio work and the internet work then it's ok. You will need to spend more money on items that should be included from Panasonic and it is best to own a newer Panasonic TV for easier installation. Panasonic kind of ruined what should be a great experience by cutting corners to save money on wire and connections. Panasonic should provide more installation on information "needs" as part of their product description if they aren't not going to provide long enough speaker wire, HDMI connectors and inputs,or audio cables,or internet Dingle or cable.
text_fidelity_b: Panasonic SC-BTT195 Energy Star 5.1-Channel 1000-Watt Full HD 3D Blu-Ray Home Theater System with Tall Boy Speakers

text_fidelity_a:
Denon D-M41 Home Theater Mini Amplifier and Bookshelf Speaker Pair - Compact HiFi Stereo System with CD, FM/AM Tuner and Wireless Bluetooth Music | Perfect for Small Rooms and Home Cinema It was time to upgrade my home stereo. I've had it for decades, and I also needed a CD player. After a bunch of research, I settled on this as a solution. Moving from a full-sized receiver and larger speakers to this was actually fairly refreshing. Here are some thoughts:

Build quality
Everything felt solid when taking it out of the box. The speakers also had a nice heft. The remote felt great, too. Once I got it set up, all the buttons had a nice feel, the volume knob was smooth, and the CD tray opened/closed in a very smooth fashion. Taking a look at the back, you have all the connections you'll need for most purposes.

Sound
I was VERY impressed at how clear this thing is. It's my first "HiFi" system, and a huge improvement over the old Aiwa/Bose system that I had. When I was gearing up to buy this, I figured I might need a small subwoofer to provide a bit of low frequency support. That's not the case at all for music! These little speakers pump out rich and full sound. I may still invest in a small sub for movies, however.

CD/Bluetooth
My primary uses for this will be for music. The CD player handles all my CDs just fine (including the "enhanced" CDs that my previous players failed to play.) Connecting this to my phone was a snap, and the Bluetooth audio sounded just fine (for Bluetooth.)

Overall, this is a little powerhouse of a system, and I can't be happier.
text_fidelity_b: Denon D-M41 Home Theater Mini Amplifier and Bookshelf Speaker Pair - Compact HiFi Stereo System with CD, FM/AM Tuner and Wireless Bluetooth Music | Perfect for Small Rooms and Home Cinema

A lot of trial-and-error to get familiar with the menu settings and customization.  Once paired and set-up, the watch worked as advertised. I contacted customer service to see what we can do about it not holding a charge so we will see what happens! The screen is still going strong! No cracks!

2017: The weight of this tablet is great and sturdy. Got for my 4 year old son so he stops breaking the screen on my iPad. It took a little getting use to but will be great for my son. I don’t feel bad if he drops it.

I got this as a Black Friday deal so it was $50. I wasn’t sure what “with special offers” meant but it sounded good so I thought “awesome! Added bonus!” Well I was greatly mistaken and that was very misleading. Maybe it is listed in the fine print but it is not easy to find. Shame on you Amazon. There are TONS of ads especially on the first screen which is annoying so I researched how to remove them. Found a YouTube video that was very helpful and found out that if I want to remove this ads (not just modify their content) I needed to pay Amazon $15 to remove them!!! I did end up paying the $15 but still really disappointed in Amazon. It’s a great product riddled with ads.

The hidden $15 removal fee for ads is why I gave this product 1 Star. I use Amazon for majority of my shopping and a loyal customer.

So if you are going to look for a table that is Amazon related, look for ones that don’t say “with special offers”!!!

text_fidelity_a:
PHILIPS 3 Ft. USB Type C Cable, USB-A to USB-C Red Durable Braided Fast Charging Cable, Compatible with iPad Pro, MacBook Pro, Samsung Galaxy S21/S10/S9/Plus, Google Pixel 5/C/3/2/XL, DLC5203RA/37 Thank you in advance to the Amazon VINE program for providing an item to review. A positive review was not required, nor was it requested, and all words are my own.

One thing I sadly use a lot of – phone/USB cables for charging and data transfer. These are almost as bad as the AUX cables for my car and iPod.

So, seeing this was a Philips one – I honestly thought I lucked out. I was going to give my old cable to my mom as hers was cracking near the "C" port. I figured I could use this one - she could have my old one.

It is a DURABLE cable and looked like it would go through quite a bit. The length is perfect for charging with an adapter connected to a power strip on the floor. And, it can also plug into the USB ports on a computer (or so equipped power strip).

So, why a one star rating?

This does not work. I tried with my phone and my mom’s phone. NADA. Nothing. I tried connecting it to the adapter – nothing. Tried using just the USB cable to a USB port on a power strip (which was on since it is powering my computer) – NOTHING.

So, I tried using a USB port on my computer. NOTHING. Tried with a “USB hub” connected to my computer. There was a slight problem. The “buttons” on the port light up when a port is turned on. Despite the port for this cord being on – the lights didn’t light up. Other items connected – my external mouse and a USB flash drive – they were turned off when this cord was connected.

Needless to say – this is BELOW one star. It doesn’t even work. But, I do have to rate it something.

I could’ve gotten a bad cable – after all, there is no damage to it or the packaging. But, it still doesn't work. But, I can’t return it since it was free.
text_fidelity_b: PHILIPS 3 Ft. USB Type C Cable, USB-A to USB-C Red Durable Braided Fast Charging Cable, Compatible with iPad Pro, MacBook Pro, Samsung Galaxy S21/S10/S9/Plus, Google Pixel 5/C/3/2/XL, DLC5203RA/37

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech Tablet Mouse for Android 3.1+ You just cannot go wrong with a Logitech mouse, and this one is no exception. Sleek and sexy, well-designed and reliable, this tablet mouse for Android 3.1+ is a joy to hold. I love the color, too. It reminds me of my beloved old teal Logitech corded mouse that wouldn't work with the newer computers. This is a notebook-sized mouse, which is the size I prefer. It is not as tiny as some of the little mice out there, though. Not too big, not to small; just right.

Logitech stresses that this is an Android mouse and that it's not going to work properly with anything older than Android 3.1. It's even in the product title, so it's obvious that the OS is important, but I'm sure there will be people out there who will think it's going to work with earlier versions of Android. I wouldn't chance it. Some other reviewers have reported successfully pairing this mouse with non-Android systems, but I haven't been able to. It did happily meet and greet a friend's tablet PC, however.

Note that, unlike some Logitech mice, this mouse does NOT have a dongle, so you must have a bluetooth-enabled machine to use it. I tried it with a generic bluetooth dongle on my Windows Vista laptop, and I couldn't get it to work. That's not the mouse's fault. One good thing about it is that you can use it with a bluetooth keyboard; if I were going to get one, I'd go with Logitech's keyboard so I know they'll play nice.

I haven't had the opportunity to run down the batteries of this mouse, but if this one is like the other Logitech mice I own, the batteries last a long, long time--unlike competitors' mice, which seem to chew up and spit out batteries every few weeks. You can turn the mouse off, of course, but the sleep function also conserves batteries. Very nice.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Tablet Mouse for Android 3.1+

text_fidelity_a:
Panasonic DMP-BDT230 Smart Wi-Fi 3D Blu-Ray Player (2013 Model) The good:

Streaming is awesome. It doesn't hiccup or give any trouble, not even with the new Super HD format from Netflix. It has the normal selection, Hulu, Amazon, Netflix, Vudu, and they all work trouble free.

It has an Ethernet port and built-in WiFi, so you can connect to the Internet however works for you.

Setup is fast and easy. It's light weight and has about as small a footprint as I've seen on such a device. Definitely good for those tight on space in their entertainment center.

The bad:

The player is slow. It takes me an average of 30 seconds to a minute from the time I press the power button to the time I can watch the disk that's already in the drive.

The UI is clunky and hard to get used to. Things just don't do what standard UI design suggests they should do. You'll get used to it in time, but it's an unnecessary learning curve.

The UI allows for customization, but it is meaningless. You can't have one person's Hulu account tied to their profile, and a second person's Hulu account tied to their profile. It's just main menu color schemes and the line.

Overall, it's a solid player, and it does everything it needs to do. If you like the features, they are exactly as described. Just be aware of the delay in launching any disks or streaming sources.
text_fidelity_b: Panasonic DMP-BDT230 Smart Wi-Fi 3D Blu-Ray Player (2013 Model)

text_fidelity_a:
Cat8 Ethernet Cable 50FT, JEVIT Internet Network Cord, 40Gbps 2000Mhz LAN Wires, High Speed S/FTP LAN Cables with Gold Plated RJ45 Connector for Router, Modem, Gaming (15m/ 50FT） Keep in mind that since this has a PVC jacket, and since PVC produces toxic smoke, this shouldn't be run from room to room (per code) despite its long length.

Also keep in mind that cat8 doesn't do anything above cat6 unless you have a 10 or 40Gb/s NIC/SFP at both ends of your link, and the total link length is shorter than it was with cat6.

So unless you need a strong backbone link in a data center, don't think you need this.

If you are running a data center, you may want to look elsewhere: this cable appears to be hand wrapped. The connectors were pushed into the body of the roll in a way where the bend radius was dangerously close to being exceeded. I guess there's something to be said for buying the best if you're really using this for business.

Just know what you need and what you're going to do with it. For almost all home applications running from room to room, I'd take a cat6 cable with a legitimate riser or plenum rating any day.
text_fidelity_b: Cat8 Ethernet Cable 50FT, JEVIT Internet Network Cord, 40Gbps 2000Mhz LAN Wires, High Speed S/FTP LAN Cables with Gold Plated RJ45 Connector for Router, Modem, Gaming (15m/ 50FT）

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech M510 Wireless Computer Mouse – Comfortable Shape with USB Unifying Receiver, with Back/Forward Buttons and Side-to-Side Scrolling, Dark Gray Having wasted many dollars on Microsoft Bluetooth mice that needed to be re-paired every time I started the computer, I settled on this Logitech series of wireless mice that use a simple, tiny wireless receiver that ALWAYS works, regardless of computer.

The first model I bought was the [[ASIN:B002HWRJBC Logitech Wireless Anywhere Mouse MX]]. It's more designed for portability and I use it on my laptops because it stores the receiver in the mouse itself and has a large convenient on/off slide switch that covers the laser when not in use. It also has a little zipper pouch for safe protected transport. Its only downside is that it's a bit small for my hands. Good for portability, slightly small for hands.

This M510 is larger, does not store the same tiny unified receiver, and does not have a zipper storage pouch. It's designed for permanent desktop use. It does have a small on/off switch on the bottom. When you first turn it on, a green LED lights on top, then goes out after a few seconds. There is no visible laser coming out the bottom. It runs on two included AA cells.

The Logitech keyboard/mouse software allows a lot of customization. All the button functions are changeable via the Logitech software.

One of the great features of both the Anywhere mouse and this M510 is the tilting wheel that allows for horizontal scrolling. Roll the wheel, it goes up and down. Tilt the wheel left or right and it scrolls left or right. Great for web windows that are larger than your screen magnification. I got so used to this feature on my laptop that I needed to get a new mouse for my desktops and the M510 fit the bill.

If you press/click the wheel down, the software goes into autoscroll mode. Depending on the window, the autoscroll may go only up and down or in all four directions. Click again or click the left mouse button and you're back to normal.

This M510 is definitely a "righthanders" mouse as the Forward/Back button are on the left side above the right thumb. It is just the right size and is very comfortable to use, gliding effortlessly on my mousepad, tracking reliably and never losing connection. Whatever RF or other wireless connection Logitech uses, it works great. The receiver is so small it's almost invisible. Little larger than the silver metal end of a USB plug. (By comparison the MS Bluetooth receiver was about 2" long and it wasn't long before the thing was broken off in my laptop. Way too big, not to mention unreliable. And it wore out the USB socket to boot.)

I was a bit concerned about the wireless receiver being recognized by my KVM switch that allows me to control two computers with one keyboard and mouse, but it's as reliable and seamless as my original corded Microsoft mouse.

One of my complaints about the Microsoft mouse was that the back button on the side was so sensitive that I would inadvertently hit it moving from the keyboard to the mouse, sometimes dumping my input. This M510 has the buttons just right. They're small and you have to find them on purpose to activate them, but they're right where they need to be and have enough resistance that they don't get actuated accidentally.

The mouse is very "grippable" and is very comfortable to use. My old Microsoft mouse was all plastic with no rubber, very slippery and hard to grip. And of course it was corded. It's amazing how "freeing" the lack of a cord is. The mouse is just "there" and not tangling on anything.

Overall, a great mouse. Love it.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech M510 Wireless Computer Mouse – Comfortable Shape with USB Unifying Receiver, with Back/Forward Buttons and Side-to-Side Scrolling, Dark Gray
